# 12-Week General Strength Programme: Post-Discectomy Return to Strength

**Client Profile:** 42M, desk worker, 8 months post L4-L5 disc herniation, currently asymptomatic. Cleared for general training with restrictions on heavy spinal loading and loaded spinal flexion.

## Key Programming Principles

**Contraindicated / avoid throughout:**
- Loaded spinal flexion (conventional deadlifts from floor early on, Jefferson curls, weighted sit-ups, loaded good mornings, behind-the-neck pressing)
- High-bar back squats with heavy loads early in the programme
- Bent-over barbell rows with heavy loads
- Russian twists with load, crunches under load

**Prioritise:**
- Neutral-spine bracing on every lift
- Anti-extension, anti-rotation, and anti-lateral-flexion core work (McGill-style)
- Hip hinge pattern re-education before loading
- Glute and posterior chain development to offload the spine
- Hip mobility and thoracic mobility to reduce lumbar compensation

**Session structure throughout:** 5-min cardio warm-up → mobility flow → core activation (McGill Big 3) → main lifts → accessories → cooldown.

---

## PHASE 1 — Foundation & Movement Re-Patterning (Weeks 1–4)

**Goal:** Reintroduce loaded movement with bulletproof technique, build core endurance, establish hip hinge, restore work capacity. 3 sessions/week, full body.

**Core warm-up (every session):** McGill Big 3 — Curl-up 3×8s holds, side plank 2×10s/side, bird dog 2×8 reps/side. Add dead bug 2×8/side.

### Week 1

**Day A**
- Goblet squat (DB) — 3×8 (focus on neutral spine, full depth only if pain-free)
- Trap-bar deadlift, high handles, light — 3×6 (this is the key hinge re-entry tool)
- DB bench press — 3×10
- Half-kneeling cable row — 3×10/side
- Pallof press — 3×10/side
- Farmer carry — 3×30m

**Day B**
- Box squat to high box — 3×8
- Hip thrust (BB, light) — 3×10
- Standing landmine press — 3×8/side
- Chest-supported DB row — 3×10
- Side plank with reach-through — 3×8/side
- Suitcase carry — 3×20m/side

**Day C**
- Bulgarian split squat (BW or light DB) — 3×8/leg
- DB Romanian deadlift — 3×8
- Push-up (controlled tempo) — 3×AMRAP-2
- Lat pulldown, neutral grip — 3×10
- Bird dog row (light DB) — 2×8/side
- Bear crawl — 3×15m

### Week 2
Same template, add 1 rep per set on main lifts, modest load increase (~5%).

### Week 3
- Goblet squat → 3×10
- Trap-bar DL (high handles) → 4×6, slight load increase
- Bench → 4×8
- Add: cable anti-rotation chop (tall kneeling) 3×10/side

### Week 4 (deload)
Reduce volume to 2 sets per exercise, keep load. Focus on bracing quality.

---

## PHASE 2 — Strength Build (Weeks 5–8)

**Goal:** Introduce heavier loading in safe patterns, build absolute strength in hinge/squat/press without spinal stress. 4 sessions/week, upper/lower split.

### Weeks 5–6

**Lower A (hinge focus)**
- Trap-bar deadlift (low handles if hinge is clean) — 4×5
- Front-foot-elevated split squat — 3×8/leg
- BB hip thrust — 4×8
- Single-leg DB RDL — 3×8/leg
- Side plank (full) — 3×20s/side
- Pallof iso hold — 3×20s/side

**Upper A (push focus)**
- BB bench press — 4×6
- Standing landmine press — 3×8/side
- Chest-supported row — 4×8
- Half-kneeling 1-arm cable row — 3×10/side
- Dead bug w/ band — 3×8/side
- Farmer carry — 3×40m

**Lower B (squat focus)**
- Safety bar squat or front squat — 4×6 (front squat preferred — keeps torso vertical, reduces shear; SSB if available)
- Reverse lunge (DB) — 3×8/leg
- 45° back extension (no weight, glute-focused, no lumbar flexion) — 3×12
- Standing cable pull-through — 3×10
- McGill curl-up — 3×10s holds
- Suitcase carry — 3×30m/side

**Upper B (pull focus)**
- Weighted chin-up or assisted — 4×6
- DB overhead press (seated, supported) — 3×8
- Single-arm DB row — 3×10/side
- Incline DB press — 3×10
- Cable face pull — 3×15
- Anti-rotation chop — 3×10/side

### Weeks 7–8
Progress main lifts: 4×5 → 5×4 on trap-bar DL and front squat. Push to RPE 7–8. Accessories progress in reps then load.

**Watch for:** any morning stiffness, end-of-day low-back fatigue. If present, cut volume 20% next session.

---

## PHASE 3 — Strength Consolidation & Carryover (Weeks 9–12)

**Goal:** Express built strength, introduce conventional deadlift variation from blocks/rack pulls (mid-shin) if hinge mechanics are bulletproof, add work capacity. 4 sessions/week.

### Weeks 9–10

**Lower A**
- Rack pull (mid-shin, from pins) — 4×5 — **only proceed if hinge is flawless; otherwise stay with trap-bar**
- Front squat — 3×6
- BB hip thrust — 4×6
- Nordic curl eccentric or leg curl — 3×8
- Side plank w/ leg lift — 3×10/side
- Heavy farmer carry — 4×30m

**Upper A**
- BB bench — 5×5
- Weighted dip or close-grip bench — 3×8
- Pendlay row (light–moderate, strict torso) OR Meadows row — 3×8 — keep load conservative
- Chin-up — 4×6
- Pallof press — 3×12/side

**Lower B**
- Trap-bar DL — 4×5 heavy
- Walking lunge (DB) — 3×10/leg
- Single-leg hip thrust — 3×10/leg
- 45° back extension w/ light plate held at chest — 3×10
- Bird dog — 3×8/side w/ pause

**Upper B**
- Standing OHP (strict, braced) — 4×6 — **only if no lumbar discomfort; sub seated landmine press otherwise**
- Incline bench — 3×8
- Chest-supported row — 4×8
- Lat pulldown — 3×10
- Cable woodchop (light, controlled) — 3×10/side

### Week 11
Peak loads — work up to top set of 3 on trap-bar DL, front squat, bench, chin-up. Reduce accessory volume 20%.

### Week 12 (test/deload week)
Light technique sessions Mon/Wed. Optional retest on Friday: trap-bar DL 3RM, front squat 3RM, bench 3RM, chin-up max reps. Then plan next block.

---

## Recovery & Lifestyle Notes for the Trainer

- **Desk job consideration:** Programme in 2-min standing/walking breaks every 30 min. Provide him with a 5-min morning mobility routine (cat-camel unloaded, hip flexor stretch, glute bridge, bird dog) — the morning is when disc-related stiffness is highest and spinal flexion tolerance is lowest. **Avoid heavy training within 1 hour of waking.**
- **Sleep:** 7+ hours, side sleeping with pillow between knees if any residual stiffness.
- **Walking:** 7–10k steps/day target — walking is one of the best things for disc health.
- **Hydration:** 35ml/kg/day minimum — disc tissue is highly water-dependent.

## Red Flags — Stop & Reassess

- Any leg pain, numbness, tingling, or radiating symptoms
- Morning back pain >30 min
- Pain that increases session-to-session rather than fluctuating
- Loss of bracing ability under load

If any appear, pull back to Phase 1 template and reconsult physio.

## Progress Markers (track weekly)

- Trap-bar DL load × reps
- Front squat / SSB squat load × reps
- Side plank hold time
- Subjective stiffness score (0–10) on waking
- Step count

Let me know if you'd like me to break out the warm-up flows in more detail, build the nutrition piece, or adjust the split (e.g. 3 days/week throughout if his recovery is limited).

# Nutrition Component: Anti-Inflammatory Eating for Recovery & Body Composition

**Client context recap:** 42M, desk worker, post-discectomy. Likely goals alongside strength: manage systemic inflammation to support disc/soft tissue health, maintain or modestly reduce body fat (less spinal load), build lean mass to support strength gains.

## Guiding Principles

The aim isn't a restrictive "anti-inflammatory diet" — it's a Mediterranean-style pattern with emphasis on omega-3s, polyphenols, fibre, and adequate protein, while limiting the foods that consistently drive low-grade systemic inflammation. This pairs well with disc health, which depends on nutrient diffusion, hydration, and a controlled inflammatory environment.

## Daily Targets

**Calories:** Start at ~32 kcal/kg bodyweight for a desk worker training 3–4x/week. Adjust after 2 weeks based on scale trend and waist measurement. If fat loss is a goal, deficit of 300–400 kcal/day max (aggressive deficits impair recovery and connective tissue repair).

**Protein:** 1.8–2.2 g/kg bodyweight, spread across 4 meals of 0.4–0.5 g/kg each. Critical for soft tissue repair and lean mass retention in a 42-year-old. Prioritise fish (especially fatty fish), poultry, eggs, Greek yoghurt, legumes, lean red meat 1–2x/week max.

**Fats:** ~30–35% of calories, weighted toward mono- and omega-3 sources.

**Carbs:** Fill the remainder — predominantly from whole-food sources. Time the largest carb portions around training.

**Fibre:** 35–40 g/day. Drives gut health, which modulates systemic inflammation.

**Water:** 35 ml/kg/day baseline, +500 ml on training days. Discs are ~80% water — non-negotiable.

## Foods to Emphasise

**Omega-3 rich (3–4x/week minimum):**
- Salmon, mackerel, sardines, anchovies, herring
- Walnuts, chia seeds, ground flaxseed, hemp seeds

**Polyphenol-dense (daily):**
- Berries (blueberries, blackberries, raspberries) — 1 cup/day target
- Extra virgin olive oil — 2–3 tbsp/day, used cold or in low-heat cooking
- Dark leafy greens (spinach, rocket, kale, chard)
- Cruciferous veg (broccoli, cauliflower, Brussels sprouts)
- Tomatoes, peppers, onions, garlic
- Green tea, coffee (1–3 cups, avoid late afternoon)
- Dark chocolate 85%+ (20–30g/day if desired)
- Turmeric (with black pepper) and ginger — use in cooking liberally

**Other anti-inflammatory staples:**
- Beetroot (also helps blood flow / training)
- Tart cherry juice (30ml, evenings — may help sleep and DOMS)
- Fermented foods: kefir, live yoghurt, sauerkraut, kimchi (gut health → inflammation regulation)
- Legumes: lentils, chickpeas, black beans
- Whole grains: oats, quinoa, brown rice, barley
- Eggs (whole)
- Nuts and seeds (small daily handful)

## Foods to Limit / Minimise

These consistently drive inflammatory markers (CRP, IL-6) in the research:

- **Ultra-processed foods:** packaged snacks, processed meats (bacon, sausages, deli meats — limit to 1–2x/week), ready meals
- **Refined sugar and high-fructose syrups:** sugary drinks, sweets, most "low-fat" products. Aim for <25g added sugar/day
- **Refined seed/vegetable oils** used at high heat: sunflower, corn, soybean. Cook with olive oil, avocado oil, or butter/ghee
- **Refined grains:** white bread, pastries — not "banned", just deprioritised
- **Alcohol:** ≤4 units/week. Beyond this, sleep, recovery, inflammation, and protein synthesis all suffer. Worth discussing honestly with him given desk-job/social-drinking patterns
- **Deep-fried foods**

## Meal Timing Around Training

**Pre-training (60–90 min before):** Mixed meal with ~30–40g protein + moderate carbs + low fat. E.g. chicken, rice, vegetables; or Greek yoghurt with oats and berries.

**Post-training (within 60 min):** 40g protein + 60–80g carbs. E.g. salmon with sweet potato and greens; whey shake + banana + oats if no time.

**Evening:** Casein-rich slow protein helps overnight recovery — Greek yoghurt, cottage cheese, or a casein shake. Tart cherry juice here if using.

## Sample Day (around 2,400 kcal, ~190g protein — adjust to his bodyweight)

**Breakfast:** 3 whole eggs + 2 whites scrambled in olive oil, spinach, tomatoes, 1 slice rye sourdough, ½ avocado, coffee, water with lemon.

**Mid-morning:** 200g Greek yoghurt, 1 cup mixed berries, 1 tbsp ground flaxseed, small handful walnuts.

**Lunch:** 150g grilled salmon, large mixed salad (rocket, spinach, peppers, tomato, cucumber, red onion, olives) dressed with EVOO and lemon, ¾ cup cooked quinoa.

**Pre-training snack:** Apple + 2 squares 85% dark chocolate + green tea.

**Post-training dinner:** 180g chicken thigh, roasted sweet potato, broccoli and cauliflower roasted with turmeric/black pepper/garlic, drizzle of EVOO.

**Evening:** 200g cottage cheese with cinnamon and a few berries; or casein shake. 30ml tart cherry juice.

## Supplements — Evidence-Based Shortlist

Discuss with his GP if he's on any medications.

- **Omega-3 (EPA/DHA):** 2–3g combined EPA+DHA daily. The single most evidence-backed anti-inflammatory supplement. Particularly relevant if oily fish intake is <3x/week.
- **Vitamin D3:** 2,000–4,000 IU/day, ideally tested first. Desk workers are frequently deficient; low vitamin D is linked to chronic pain and poor connective tissue health.
- **Creatine monohydrate:** 5g/day. Not anti-inflammatory per se, but excellent for strength, lean mass, and increasingly for cognitive/aging benefits.
- **Whey protein:** Practical tool to hit daily protein, not a requirement.
- **Magnesium glycinate:** 300–400mg evening — sleep quality, muscle relaxation. Useful given his back history.
- **Curcumin (with piperine or as Meriva/BCM-95):** 500mg 1–2x/day. Modest but real evidence for reducing inflammation and joint/back discomfort. Worth a 12-week trial.
- **Collagen peptides:** 15–20g + 50mg vitamin C, taken 30–60 min pre-training. Emerging evidence for connective tissue support — relevant for disc/spinal ligaments.

**Not recommended without specific indication:** high-dose antioxidant stacks (can blunt training adaptations), exotic herbal blends, anti-inflammatory megadoses.

## Behavioural Implementation

For a desk worker, friction is the enemy. Help him with:

1. **Meal prep 2x/week** — Sunday and Wednesday. Cook 3 protein sources, 2 carbs, 2 veg in bulk.
2. **Default lunch template** at work — protein + greens + carb + EVOO. Removes daily decision-making.
3. **Hydration cue** — 750ml water bottle on desk, refill 3x/day visible target.
4. **One "free" meal per week** — flexibility prevents the pattern collapsing. Not a "cheat day" — a planned meal out.
5. **Caffeine cut-off:** 2pm. Sleep quality is foundational to inflammation control.

## Tracking & Adjustments

- **Weekly:** Bodyweight (morning, 3x/week average), waist at navel, energy 1–10, sleep quality 1–10, training performance, any back stiffness 1–10.
- **Every 4 weeks (aligning with programme phases):** Adjust calories if scale trend isn't matching goal. Reassess fish intake, alcohol, sugar — these are the three highest-leverage levers.
- **Optional bloodwork** (suggest via GP) at week 0 and week 12: hsCRP, vitamin D, HbA1c, lipid panel, ferritin. Gives objective feedback on the anti-inflammatory pattern.

Let me know if you'd like a printable client handout version, a shopping list, or want me to build out specific meal preps for him.

# Cardio Addition: 2x/Week Across the 12-Week Programme

**Rationale for this client:** Improves disc nutrition (cyclical loading drives fluid exchange in the disc), supports the anti-inflammatory nutrition plan, manages bodyweight (reducing spinal load), improves work capacity for strength sessions, and counters the cardiovascular cost of a desk job. Walking and cycling are particularly disc-friendly; running is reintroduced cautiously and only if mechanics and symptoms permit.

## Programming Principles

- **Avoid high-impact work early** — running, jumping, rowing under fatigue all stress the lumbar spine. Build the base first.
- **Rowing machine — use with caution.** It's a loaded hip hinge under fatigue; form breaks down and lumbar flexion creeps in. We'll only use it later, short duration, with strict form. Bike, incline walking, and elliptical are safer defaults.
- **Schedule cardio away from heavy lower-body lifts** where possible. Use Zone 2 on rest days or after upper-body sessions; reserve harder intervals for non-lifting days.
- **Two modalities per week:** one longer Zone 2 session (aerobic base, recovery-promoting) and one shorter higher-intensity session (VO2/work capacity).

## Weekly Schedule Template

Once we move to the 4-day split in Phase 2, the week looks like this:

| Day | Session |
|---|---|
| Mon | Lower A |
| Tue | Upper A + optional short Zone 2 (20 min easy bike) |
| Wed | **Cardio 1 — Zone 2 (longer)** |
| Thu | Lower B |
| Fri | Upper B |
| Sat | **Cardio 2 — Intervals (shorter)** |
| Sun | Rest / walk |

In Phase 1 (3 lifting days), cardio slots into 2 of the 4 non-lifting days, with the remaining days as walking/mobility.

## Heart Rate Zones (estimate for a 42-year-old)

- **Zone 2 (aerobic base):** ~115–135 bpm, or "could hold a conversation but wouldn't want to". RPE 4–5/10.
- **Zone 4 (threshold/intervals):** ~150–165 bpm. RPE 8/10.
- **Zone 5 (VO2):** ~165–175 bpm. RPE 9/10. Used sparingly.

If he has a chest strap or watch, use HR. Otherwise, RPE and the talk test work fine.

---

## PHASE 1 — Weeks 1–4: Aerobic Base & Reintroduction

**Goal:** Build aerobic capacity with zero spinal stress. Both sessions are low-impact.

### Cardio Session 1 — Zone 2 (Wednesday)
- **Modality:** Stationary bike (upright or recumbent) or incline treadmill walk (10–12% gradient, 5–5.5 km/h)
- **Week 1:** 25 min steady
- **Week 2:** 30 min steady
- **Week 3:** 35 min steady
- **Week 4:** 30 min (deload)

### Cardio Session 2 — Light Intervals (Saturday)
- **Modality:** Stationary bike (preferred) or incline walk
- **Format:** 5 min warm-up → intervals → 5 min cool-down
- **Week 1:** 6 × (1 min moderate / 2 min easy) — RPE 6
- **Week 2:** 7 × (1 min moderate / 2 min easy) — RPE 6
- **Week 3:** 6 × (90 sec moderate / 2 min easy) — RPE 7
- **Week 4:** 5 × (1 min moderate / 2 min easy) — RPE 6 (deload)

---

## PHASE 2 — Weeks 5–8: Build Capacity

**Goal:** Extend Zone 2 duration, introduce true threshold intervals. Still no impact unless symptom-free running is being considered with physio sign-off.

### Cardio Session 1 — Zone 2 (Wednesday)
- **Modality:** Bike, incline walk outdoors, or elliptical (mix for variety)
- **Week 5:** 40 min
- **Week 6:** 45 min

# Safe & Effective Ab Work for Your Client

**Quick reframe to have with him:** Visible abs come from body fat percentage, not from ab exercises. The anti-inflammatory nutrition plan and cardio are doing the heavy lifting for visibility. What ab *training* actually does is build core thickness and improve performance/posture — both worth doing, with the right exercise selection.

## Programming Principles for His Spine

**The key concept — Stuart McGill's framework:** the lumbar spine has a finite "bending tolerance" before disc tissue is irritated. Repeated loaded flexion (crunches, sit-ups, weighted Russian twists, hanging leg raises with lumbar flexion) eats into that tolerance. Anti-movement core work builds the same musculature without spending that bending budget.

**What this means in practice:**
- **No** crunches, sit-ups, weighted decline sit-ups, V-ups, toes-to-bar, Jefferson curls
- **No** loaded Russian twists, weighted side bends, side-bending machines
- **No** GHD sit-ups, hanging leg raises that involve posterior pelvic tilt / lumbar flexion
- **Yes** to anti-extension, anti-rotation, anti-lateral-flexion, and hip-flexion-with-neutral-spine work

The good news: anti-movement core training produces excellent rectus abdominis, obliques, and transverse abdominis development. It also tends to produce a thicker, more "athletic" midsection look than endless crunches.

## Exercise Menu (All Safe for Him)

### Anti-Extension (rectus abdominis emphasis)
- **Dead bug variations** — standard, with band pull, with DB pullover, with KB hold
- **Plank** — standard, RKC-style (max tension), weighted (plate on back), long lever
- **Ab wheel rollout from knees** — only when ready; requires good control to avoid lumbar extension. Progress: kneeling partial → kneeling full → standing (advanced)
- **Stability ball rollout** (easier rollout regression)
- **Hollow body hold** — full or tucked
- **Bodysaw on sliders** — excellent progression from plank

### Anti-Rotation (obliques, deep core)
- **Pallof press** — half-kneeling, tall-kneeling, standing, split-stance
- **Pallof iso hold** with overhead reach
- **Landmine rotations to anti-rotations** (controlled, no spinal twist — movement comes from hips)
- **Bird dog** — standard, with band resistance, with DB
- **Renegade row** (light DBs, wide stance — it's an anti-rotation exercise, not a row)
- **Single-arm farmer carry / suitcase carry** — anti-lateral-flexion, but also anti-rotation

### Anti-Lateral-Flexion (obliques, QL)
- **Side plank** — standard, with leg lift, with hip dip (controlled, small ROM), star plank
- **Suitcase carry** — heavy, slow, perfect posture
- **Single-arm overhead carry** (light)
- **Copenhagen plank** — advanced, great for adductors and obliques

### Hip Flexion with Neutral Spine (lower abs — the "lower ab" feel he probably wants)
This is where most people go wrong post-injury. The cue is: **flex at the hip, not the spine.** Brace, posteriorly tilt slightly, and keep the lumbar spine glued to neutral.

- **Reverse crunch (controlled, small ROM, no momentum)** — keep low back pressed down
- **Heel taps / dead bug leg lowers** — gold standard for lower ab activation with zero spinal stress
- **Hanging knee raise** — only if he can do it without pelvic tilt at the bottom; stop the rep before the spine flexes
- **Garhammer raise** (knees up to chest, hips don't roll back) — top end of ROM only
- **Lying leg raise with hands under hips** — only with strict neutral spine

## How to Programme It

**Volume guideline:** Direct ab work 3–4x/week is plenty. More isn't better — core musculature recovers quickly but the *spine* needs recovery from cumulative bracing.

**Slot it in like this:**

### Phase 1 (Weeks 1–4)
Already in the programme via McGill Big 3 warm-ups and Pallof presses. **Don't add more.** He's rebuilding capacity.

### Phase 2 (Weeks 5–8)
Add one dedicated "ab finisher" at the end of 2 sessions per week (e.g. end of Upper A and Upper B). Keep warm-up core work too.

**Sample finisher A (5–7 min):**
- Dead bug with band — 3×8/side
- Pallof press — 3×10/side
- Side plank with reach-through — 3×8/side

**Sample finisher B (5–7 min):**
- Stability ball rollout — 3×10
- Suitcase carry heavy — 3×30m/side
- Hollow body hold — 3×20s

### Phase 3 (Weeks 9–12)
Progress to harder variations, add a third weekly finisher if recovery allows.

**Sample finisher A:**
- Ab wheel rollout (kneeling) — 3×8
- Standing Pallof press — 3×10/side
- Copenhagen plank — 3×15s/side

**Sample finisher B:**
- Bodysaw on sliders — 3×10
- Renegade row (light) — 3×6/side
- Side plank with leg lift — 3×8/side

## Progression Logic

For each anti-movement category, progress along these lines:
1. **Increase time under tension** (longer holds, slower tempo)
2. **Increase lever length** (e.g. plank → long lever plank; bent-knee dead bug → straight-leg)
3. **Add load** (plate on back, heavier carries, band resistance on Pallof/dead bug)
4. **Reduce stability** (standing variations, single-leg variations, slider work)
5. **Combine patterns** (e.g. bird dog row = anti-extension + anti-rotation)

**Don't** progress by adding spinal flexion. Ever, for him.

## Setting Expectations With Him

Tell him directly:

1. **Ab "definition" comes from the kitchen and cardio.** The programme already addresses both.
2. **He'll build genuine core strength** that protects his back and improves every lift — likely visible as a thicker, more athletic midsection within 8–12 weeks if body fat is dropping.
3. **The exercises will feel less "burny" than crunches** but they're more effective. The burn isn't the goal; tension and stability under load are.
4. **If anything in this list causes back symptoms, stop that exercise.** There are plenty of alternatives.

## Red Flags Specific to Ab Work

- Lumbar arching off the floor during dead bugs / leg raises → regress (bent knees, shorter lever)
- Hip flexor cramping dominating ab work → his bracing is breaking and hip flexors are compensating; regress and re-cue
- Any back stiffness the morning after ab work → reduce volume 30%
- Pelvic tilt at the bottom of hanging knee raises → drop the exercise, return to floor-based work

# 1RM Testing in Week 12 — Recommendations & Build-In

Before I build it, I need to flag something clearly — and then I'll give you the plan if you proceed.

## The Honest Conversation to Have With Him First

**A true 1RM test is the highest-risk single moment in a training programme.** Maximal loads, maximal bracing, maximal nervous system output, and — critically — the highest likelihood of form breakdown at the limit. For a client 11 months post-discectomy, this needs careful thought.

**My recommendation:** Don't test a true 1RM. Instead, test a **3RM and calculate estimated 1RM.** Here's why:

- A 3RM gives ~93% of 1RM data — almost identical for tracking progress
- The risk profile is dramatically lower: bracing holds better, form is more honest, and there's a clear "you've got nothing left" signal before failure
- He's been training for 12 weeks, not 12 years — his 1RM technique under maximal load is unproven
- A failed 1RM (form breakdown, dropped bar, twist under load) at this stage could undo the entire programme's progress
- His physio cleared him for training, not for maximal testing — worth a quick check-in before any true 1RM

**If he insists on a true 1RM after that conversation**, I'll build it — but with hard rules and lift selection that respect his history.

**Safe to test (1RM or 3RM):**
- **Trap-bar deadlift** — neutral grip, load centered, far safer than conventional. This is his best maximal test option.
- **Front squat** — self-limiting (if form breaks, the bar drops forward off the shoulders before the spine is loaded badly). Excellent test choice.
- **Bench press** — lowest spinal risk of the main lifts. Test freely.
- **Weighted chin-up** — test max reps at a set load, or 3RM added weight.

**Do NOT test:**
- **Conventional deadlift** — never been in the programme, not tested under load, highest spinal shear of any lift
- **Back squat** — not in the programme; first heavy attempt under fatigue at end of 12 weeks is not the time
- **Overhead press 1RM** — high lumbar extension demand at limit; 3RM if he wants this one
- **Rack pull 1RM** — was introduced in Phase 3 but not built for max effort

1. **Form is the lift, not the load.** If bracing breaks, bar speed dies, or spine position is lost mid-rep, the attempt doesn't count and we don't go heavier. Full stop.

3. **No belt-only saves.** A belt assists bracing; it doesn't fix a broken hinge. If he can't brace without a belt at 80%, he doesn't test.

- A grinding, form-broken 1RM at a "PR" weight = failure, regardless of what the bar weighs

# Sleep & Recovery Protocol

For a 42-year-old desk worker, post-discectomy, training 4x/week with cardio and pushing intensity — recovery is the limiting factor, not the training. Most clients in this profile under-recover before they under-train. This protocol addresses sleep (the biggest lever), nervous system recovery, soft tissue care, and specifically lumbar disc health.

## Why This Matters For Him Specifically

- **Disc tissue repair and nutrient diffusion happen primarily during sleep** when the spine is unloaded and rehydrating
- **Growth hormone release peaks in deep sleep** — directly drives soft tissue recovery and muscle repair
- **Inflammation regulation is sleep-dependent** — poor sleep raises CRP and IL-6, undermining the entire anti-inflammatory nutrition strategy
- **Bracing quality degrades sharply with sleep deprivation** — increases injury risk in his lifts
- **At 42, hormonal recovery (testosterone, cortisol regulation) is more sleep-dependent than it was at 25**

## Sleep Foundation

### Duration
**Target: 7.5–8.5 hours in bed, 7+ hours actual sleep.** Below 7 hours, every recovery marker suffers. Below 6 hours for 2+ consecutive nights, training intensity must drop the following day — non-negotiable.

### Consistency
**Same bed time and wake time, ±30 min, including weekends.** Circadian regularity matters more than total hours. A consistent 7-hour sleeper recovers better than an erratic 8-hour sleeper.

### Sleep Environment
- **Temperature: 16–19°C.** Cooler than feels intuitive. The body needs to drop core temp to enter deep sleep.
- **Complete darkness.** Blackout curtains or sleep mask. Even small amounts of ambient light reduce melatonin production.
- **Quiet or consistent low noise.** White noise machine or app if his environment is noisy.
- **Mattress check given his back history.** Medium-firm is generally optimal for disc issues. If his current mattress is over 8 years old or he wakes with significant stiffness, this is worth investing in. A pillow between the knees (side sleeping) or under the knees (back sleeping) reduces lumbar load overnight.
- **Sleep position:** Side sleeping with knees slightly bent and pillow between them is gold-standard for him. Back sleeping with pillow under knees is fine. Prone (stomach) sleeping should be avoided — it forces lumbar extension and neck rotation.

### Pre-Sleep Protocol (90 min before bed)
- **No screens, or use blue-light filtering** (glasses or device settings)
- **Lights dimmed** throughout the home — signals melatonin onset
- **No food** within 2 hrs of bed (exception: the casein/cottage cheese pre-bed protein already in the nutrition plan — small portion, low impact)
- **No alcohol within 3 hrs of bed** — alcohol destroys sleep architecture even if it speeds sleep onset
- **Caffeine cut-off: 2pm** (already in nutrition plan — caffeine has a 6-hour half-life; a 4pm coffee still has 50% in his system at 10pm)
- **Hot shower or bath 60–90 min before bed** — paradoxically aids sleep onset (the post-bath temperature drop signals sleep readiness)
- **Bedroom is for sleep only** — no work, no TV. Conditions the brain.

### Pre-Sleep Wind-Down (15–20 min before bed)
A simple routine he can actually do:
- Light mobility: cat-camel (unloaded), 90/90 hip stretch, child's pose, supine knees-to-chest (gentle)
- 5 min of box breathing (4 sec in / 4 hold / 4 out / 4 hold) or simple slow nasal breathing
- Reading (physical book or e-reader on warm light)

This downregulates the nervous system — particularly important on training days when he's still sympathetically activated from the session.

## Daily Recovery Practices

### Morning Routine (10 min)
Critical for him given disc-related morning stiffness:
- **Wait 30+ min after waking before any spinal flexion or significant loading.** Disc tissue is most hydrated and most vulnerable in the first hour after waking — McKenzie protocol research is clear on this
- 5 min easy walk around the house, get sunlight in eyes if possible
- Cat-camel (unloaded) × 8 slow reps
- Glute bridge × 10
- Bird dog × 5/side
- Hip flexor stretch × 30s/side
- Standing thoracic rotations × 8/side
- Then breakfast, coffee, etc.

**Sunlight exposure within 30 min of waking — 10 min minimum, outdoors if possible.** Single biggest lever for circadian regulation, which feeds back into sleep quality that night.

### Desk-Day Recovery (during work hours)
The desk job is fighting his recovery all day. Counter it:
- **Stand or walk every 30 min** — 2-minute reset. Set a timer.
- **Walking after meals** — 10 min after each major meal, already in the plan. Doubles as glucose management and lumbar mobility.
- **Hydration target** visible on desk — disc tissue needs water
- **Hip flexor stretch + thoracic rotation** at lunch — 3 min, takes the pressure off the lumbar spine from sitting
- **Avoid the slouched-into-flexion posture** when fatigued in the afternoon. Standing desk for the second half of the day if available.

### Evening Routine
- **Walk after dinner** — 15–20 min easy. Lowers cortisol, improves sleep onset, supports digestion.
- **Light mobility** as part of the wind-down protocol above
- **Mental decompression** — not necessarily meditation, but no work emails after 8pm

## Per-Session Recovery

### Pre-Training
- **Adequate warm-up** is recovery work — saves him recovery time later by reducing micro-injury
- **Hydration:** 500 ml water in the 2 hours before training, sipping not chugging
- **Caffeine** 30–45 min pre-training if used (and before the 2pm cut-off) — improves bracing quality and bar speed

### Intra-Training
- **Rest periods on main lifts: 2.5–3.5 min minimum** in Phase 2 and 3. Cutting rest to "feel the burn" wrecks bracing on subsequent sets — particularly dangerous for him
- **Don't skip the warm-up ramp-up sets** even when feeling good. Cold heavy lifts are how backs get tweaked.

### Post-Training (within 60 min)
- **Refeed** per nutrition plan — 40g protein + 60–80g carbs
- **5–10 min easy walk or bike** as cooldown — flushes the nervous system, transitions from sympathetic to parasympathetic
- **Decompression position** — supine, knees bent over a bench or chair, 2–3 min. Lets the lumbar spine offload after heavy lifting.

### Same Evening
- Extra emphasis on the wind-down protocol on training nights — his nervous system is more activated and needs more help downregulating
- Magnesium glycinate 300–400 mg (already in supplement list) particularly useful on training days

**The Sunday rest day is sacred.** No gym, no cardio. 30–40 min walk, mobility, food prep, downtime. This is where the previous week's training actually consolidates.

## Soft Tissue & Mobility Work

Not strictly necessary for recovery — but useful and easy to programme:

### Daily (5 min total)
- Cat-camel × 8
- 90/90 hip mobility × 5/side
- Thoracic rotation × 8/side
- Glute bridge × 10

### 2x/week longer session (15–20 min)
- Foam roller: quads, glutes, lats, upper back (**not** directly on lumbar spine — roll the surrounding tissue, not the affected disc area)
- Lacrosse ball: glutes, pecs, calves
- Dynamic stretching: hip flexors, hamstrings, thoracic spine
- Couch stretch — particularly valuable for desk workers

**What to avoid:** Aggressive lumbar foam rolling, deep tissue work directly on the lower back, end-range loaded stretching of the spine. If he wants hands-on work, a qualified sports massage therapist who has his medical history — not a generic deep tissue session.

## Sauna / Cold Exposure (Optional)

If he has access and is interested:

- **Sauna 2–3x/week, 15–20 min sessions at 80–90°C.** Evidence is strong for cardiovascular benefits, recovery, and (relevant here) reduction of chronic inflammation markers. Best used post-training or on non-training evenings.
- **Cold exposure (cold shower or plunge):** 2–3 min, 2–3x/week. **Avoid immediately after strength training** (within 4 hrs) — blunts hypertrophy adaptations. Use on rest days or mornings instead. Good for mental resilience and possible anti-inflammatory effects, but lower priority than sleep and walking.

These are *nice-to-haves*. Sleep, walking, and hydration are *must-haves*. Don't let him chase exotic recovery modalities while sleeping 6 hours and skipping post-meal walks.

### Decision Rules from Tracking

These give you clear thresholds, not guesswork:

- **Readiness <5** on a lifting day → switch to technique session at 60% loads
- **Morning back stiffness >5 for 2 consecutive days** → drop the next lower-body session intensity by 15% and reassess
- **Sleep <6 hrs for 2 nights** → cardio interval session that week becomes Zone 2
- **Resting HR up 7+ bpm vs his baseline** → systemic under-recovery, full deload that week
- **Three consecutive amber flags in a week** → unscheduled deload week, return to Phase 1 template

This isn't paranoid programming — it's the difference between a client who completes 12 weeks and a client who tweaks his back in Week 9.

- Increasing morning stiffness across a week despite no programming changes → systemic recovery deficit, deload
- Sleep onset taking >30 min when it normally doesn't → sympathetic overload, look at evening caffeine/alcohol/screens/training timing
- Waking at 3–4am consistently → often cortisol dysregulation, often driven by training too late, alcohol, or under-eating
- Feeling worse after rest days, not better → may be undereating on rest days (common mistake — appetite drops but recovery demand doesn't)
- Persistent low mood, irritability, loss of motivation → classic overreaching signs, takes longer to surface than physical markers

# PART 1: PROGRAMMING PRINCIPLES

## Contraindicated / Avoid Throughout

- Loaded spinal flexion (conventional deadlifts from floor early on, Jefferson curls, weighted sit-ups, loaded good mornings, behind-the-neck pressing)
- High-bar back squats with heavy loads
- Bent-over barbell rows with heavy loads
- Russian twists with load, crunches under load
- Crunches, sit-ups, V-ups, toes-to-bar, Jefferson curls, GHD sit-ups
- Conventional deadlift max testing
- Prone (stomach) sleeping

## Prioritise

- Neutral-spine bracing on every lift
- Anti-extension, anti-rotation, anti-lateral-flexion core work
- Hip hinge pattern re-education before loading
- Glute and posterior chain development
- Hip and thoracic mobility

## Universal Session Structure

5-min cardio warm-up → mobility flow → core activation (McGill Big 3) → main lifts → accessories → 5–10 min cooldown walk → decompression position 2–3 min

## RPE Reference (Phase 2+)

- RPE 7: 3 reps in reserve, comfortable
- RPE 8: 2 reps in reserve, hard but clean
- RPE 8.5: 1–2 reps in reserve, fast bar speed maintained
- RPE 9: 1 rep in reserve, real grind

If bar speed visibly slows or bracing degrades, the set ends — regardless of rep count.

# 12-Week General Strength Programme — Master Document
## Post-Discectomy Return to Strength

**Client:** 42M, desk worker, 8 months post L4-L5 disc herniation, currently asymptomatic. Cleared by physio for training with restrictions on heavy spinal loading and loaded spinal flexion.

**Programme Goals:** Build general strength, restore work capacity, improve body composition, support long-term spine health.

**Programme Structure:**
- Phase 1 (Weeks 1–4): Foundation & Movement Re-Patterning — 3 sessions/week, full body
- Phase 2 (Weeks 5–8): Strength Build with Intensity Push — 4 sessions/week, upper/lower split
- Phase 3 (Weeks 9–12): Strength Consolidation & 3RM Test — 4 sessions/week, upper/lower split

---

# PART 1: PROGRAMMING PRINCIPLES

## Contraindicated / Avoid Throughout

- Loaded spinal flexion (conventional deadlifts from floor early on, Jefferson curls, weighted sit-ups, loaded good mornings, behind-the-neck pressing)
- High-bar back squats with heavy loads
- Bent-over barbell rows with heavy loads
- Russian twists with load, crunches under load
- Crunches, sit-ups, V-ups, toes-to-bar, Jefferson curls, GHD sit-ups
- Conventional deadlift max testing
- Prone (stomach) sleeping

## Prioritise

- Neutral-spine bracing on every lift
- Anti-extension, anti-rotation, anti-lateral-flexion core work
- Hip hinge pattern re-education before loading
- Glute and posterior chain development
- Hip and thoracic mobility

## Universal Session Structure

5-min cardio warm-up → mobility flow → core activation (McGill Big 3) → main lifts → accessories → 5–10 min cooldown walk → decompression position 2–3 min

## RPE Reference (Phase 2+)

- RPE 7: 3 reps in reserve, comfortable
- RPE 8: 2 reps in reserve, hard but clean
- RPE 8.5: 1–2 reps in reserve, fast bar speed maintained
- RPE 9: 1 rep in reserve, real grind

If bar speed visibly slows or bracing degrades, the set ends — regardless of rep count.

---

# PART 2: PHASE 1 — FOUNDATION (WEEKS 1–4)

3 sessions/week (Day A / Day B / Day C). Cardio 2x/week on non-lifting days.

**Core warm-up every session:** McGill Big 3 — Curl-up 3×8s holds, side plank 2×10s/side, bird dog 2×8/side. Add dead bug 2×8/side.

## Week 1

**Day A**
- Goblet squat (DB) — 3×8
- Trap-bar deadlift, high handles, light — 3×6
- DB bench press — 3×10
- Half-kneeling cable row — 3×10/side
- Pallof press — 3×10/side
- Farmer carry — 3×30m

**Day B**
- Box squat to high box — 3×8
- Hip thrust (BB, light) — 3×10
- Standing landmine press — 3×8/side
- Chest-supported DB row — 3×10
- Side plank with reach-through — 3×8/side
- Suitcase carry — 3×20m/side

**Day C**
- Bulgarian split squat (BW/light DB) — 3×8/leg
- DB Romanian deadlift — 3×8
- Push-up (controlled tempo) — 3×AMRAP-2
- Lat pulldown, neutral grip — 3×10
- Bird dog row (light DB) — 2×8/side
- Bear crawl — 3×15m

**Cardio Session 1 (Wed):** 25 min Zone 2 — stationary bike or incline walk (10–12% gradient, 5–5.5 km/h)

**Cardio Session 2 (Sat):** 5 min warm-up + 6 × (1 min moderate / 2 min easy) + 5 min cool-down — bike or incline walk

## Week 2

Same exercise template as Week 1. Add 1 rep per set on main lifts, modest load increase (~5%).

**Cardio 1:** 30 min Zone 2
**Cardio 2:** 7 × (1 min moderate / 2 min easy)

## Week 3

**Day A**
- Goblet squat → 3×10
- Trap-bar DL (high handles) → 4×6
- DB bench press → 4×8
- Half-kneeling cable row → 3×10/side
- Pallof press → 3×10/side
- Add: cable anti-rotation chop (tall kneeling) — 3×10/side
- Farmer carry — 3×30m

**Day B**
- Box squat → 3×10
- BB hip thrust → 4×10
- Landmine press → 3×8/side
- Chest-supported row → 3×10
- Side plank with reach-through → 3×8/side
- Suitcase carry — 3×20m/side

**Day C**
- Bulgarian split squat → 3×10/leg
- DB Romanian deadlift → 3×10
- Push-up → 3×AMRAP-2
- Lat pulldown → 3×10
- Bird dog row → 3×8/side
- Bear crawl — 3×15m

**Cardio 1:** 35 min Zone 2
**Cardio 2:** 6 × (90 sec moderate / 2 min easy)

## Week 4 (Deload)

Reduce volume to 2 sets per exercise, keep load. Focus on bracing quality.

**Cardio 1:** 30 min Zone 2
**Cardio 2:** 5 × (1 min moderate / 2 min easy)

---

# PART 3: PHASE 2 — STRENGTH BUILD WITH INTENSITY PUSH (WEEKS 5–8)

4 sessions/week, upper/lower split. Cardio 2x/week.

## Weekly Template

| Day | Session |
|---|---|
| Mon | Lower A |
| Tue | Upper A |
| Wed | Cardio 1 (Zone 2) |
| Thu | Lower B |
| Fri | Upper B |
| Sat | Cardio 2 (Intervals) |
| Sun | Rest (walk, mobility) |

## Weeks 5–6

### Lower A (Hinge Focus)
- Trap-bar deadlift (low handles if hinge is clean) — work up to 1×4 @ RPE 8, then 3×5 @ ~85%
- Front-foot-elevated split squat — 4×6/leg
- BB hip thrust — top set 1×6 @ RPE 8, then 3×8 back-off
- Single-leg DB RDL — 3×8/leg
- Side plank (full) — 3×25s/side
- Pallof iso hold — 3×25s/side

### Upper A (Push Focus)
- BB bench press — work up to 1×4 @ RPE 8, then 3×6 @ ~85%
- Standing landmine press — 4×6/side
- Chest-supported row — 4×8
- Half-kneeling 1-arm cable row — 3×10/side
- Dead bug w/ band — 3×8/side
- Farmer carry — 3×40m, heavy
- **Finisher (Week 6+):** Dead bug w/ band 3×8/side, Pallof press 3×10/side, side plank with reach-through 3×8/side

### Lower B (Squat Focus)
- Front squat (or SSB) — work up to 1×4 @ RPE 8, then 3×5 @ ~85%
- Reverse lunge (DB) — 4×8/leg
- 45° back extension (BW, glute-focused, no lumbar flexion) — 3×15
- Standing cable pull-through — 3×10
- McGill curl-up — 3×10s holds
- Suitcase carry — 3×30m/side

### Upper B (Pull Focus)
- Weighted chin-up — top set 1×4 @ RPE 8, then 3×6 back-off
- DB OHP (seated, supported) — 4×6
- Single-arm DB row — 4×8/side
- Incline DB press — 3×8
- Cable face pull — 3×15
- Anti-rotation chop — 3×10/side
- **Finisher (Week 6+):** Stability ball rollout 3×10, suitcase carry heavy 3×30m/side, hollow body hold 3×20s

**Cardio Week 5:**
- Wed: 40 min Zone 2
- Sat: 5 × (2 min hard / 2 min easy) at RPE 8

**Cardio Week 6:**
- Wed: 45 min Zone 2
- Sat: 6 × (2 min hard / 2 min easy) at RPE 8

## Weeks 7–8 (Intensity Peak of Phase 2)

### Lower A
- Trap-bar deadlift — work up to 1×3 @ RPE 8.5–9, then 2×4 @ ~85%
- Front-foot-elevated split squat — 4×6/leg
- BB hip thrust — top set 1×5 @ RPE 8.5, then 2×6 back-off
- Single-leg DB RDL — 3×8/leg
- Side plank with leg lift — 3×10/side
- Pallof press — 3×12/side

### Upper A
- BB bench press — work up to 1×3 @ RPE 8.5–9, then 2×5 @ ~85%
- Standing landmine press — 4×6/side
- Chest-supported row — 4×8 heavy
- Half-kneeling cable row — 3×10/side
- Dead bug w/ band — 3×10/side
- Heavy farmer carry — 4×40m
- **Finisher:** Dead bug w/ band 3×10/side, Pallof press 3×12/side, side plank with leg lift 3×10/side

### Lower B
- Front squat — work up to 1×3 @ RPE 8.5–9, then 2×4 @ ~85%
- Reverse lunge (DB) — 4×8/leg
- 45° back extension w/ light plate — 3×12
- Standing cable pull-through — 3×10
- Stability ball rollout — 3×10
- Suitcase carry — 3×30m/side

### Upper B
- Weighted chin-up — top set 1×3 @ RPE 8.5, then 2×5 back-off
- DB OHP — 4×5
- Single-arm DB row — 4×8/side
- Incline DB press — 3×8
- Face pull — 3×15
- Anti-rotation chop — 3×10/side
- **Finisher:** Stability ball rollout 3×10, suitcase carry heavy 3×30m/side, hollow body hold 3×25s

**Cardio Week 7:**
- Wed: 50 min Zone 2
- Sat: 3 × (3 min hard / 2 min easy) — **reduced from original to accommodate lifting intensity**

**Cardio Week 8 (deload):**

- Sat: 4 × (2 min hard / 2 min easy) at RPE 6

**Phase 2 Recovery Adjustments:**
- +150–200 kcal on heavy lifting days (carbs around training)
- Sleep 7.5+ hrs non-negotiable
- Add extra ramp-up set on every main lift before working sets

---

# PART 4: PHASE 3 — STRENGTH CONSOLIDATION & TESTING (WEEKS 9–12)

Same weekly template as Phase 2. Phase 3 intensity is *moderated* given the harder Phase 2 — we ramp gradually to peak in Week 11, then test in Week 12.

## Weeks 9–10

### Lower A
- Trap-bar deadlift — work up to 1×4 @ RPE 7–8, then 3×5 @ ~85%
- Rack pull (mid-shin, from pins) — 3×5 @ RPE 7 — **only if hinge is bulletproof; otherwise sub more trap-bar volume**
- BB hip thrust — 4×6
- Nordic curl eccentric or leg curl — 3×8
- Side plank w/ leg lift — 3×10/side

### Upper A
- BB bench — work up to 1×4 @ RPE 7–8, then 3×5 @ ~85%
- Weighted dip or close-grip bench — 3×8
- Pendlay row (light–moderate, strict torso) OR Meadows row — 3×8
- Chin-up — 4×6
- Pallof press — 3×12/side
- **Finisher:** Ab wheel rollout (kneeling) 3×8, standing Pallof press 3×10/side, Copenhagen plank 3×15s/side

### Lower B
- Front squat — work up to 1×4 @ RPE 7–8, then 3×5 @ ~85%
- Walking lunge (DB) — 3×10/leg

### Upper B

- Incline bench — 3×8
- Chest-supported row — 4×8
- Lat pulldown — 3×10
- Cable woodchop (light, controlled) — 3×10/side
- **Finisher:** Bodysaw on sliders 3×10, renegade row (light) 3×6/side, side plank with leg lift 3×8/side

**Cardio Week 9:**
- Wed: 50 min Zone 2
- Sat: 6 × (90 sec hard at RPE 9 / 2 min easy)

**Cardio Week 10:**
- Wed: 55 min Zone 2
- Sat: 8 × (90 sec hard / 2 min easy)

**Optional from Week 9:** Walk-run reintroduction in place of Wed Zone 2, if asymptomatic and physio happy:
- Week 9: 5 × (2 min jog / 3 min walk)
- Week 10: 5 × (3 min jog / 2 min walk)

## Week 11 — Peak/Test Rehearsal

**Critical: top sets in Week 11 = RPE 8, max. These set the test-day openers. NO max attempts this week.**

### Lower A (Monday)
- Trap-bar DL — work up to 1×3 @ RPE 8 *(opener indicator)*
- Front-foot-elevated split squat — 3×6/leg
- BB hip thrust — 3×6
- Single-leg RDL — 2×8/leg
- Pallof press — 3×10/side

### Upper A (Tuesday)
- BB bench — work up to 1×3 @ RPE 8 *(opener indicator)*

- Chest-supported row — 3×8

**Wed Cardio:** 45 min easy Zone 2 only. No intervals.

### Lower B (Thursday)
- Front squat — work up to 1×3 @ RPE 8 *(opener indicator)*
- Reverse lunge — 3×6/leg
- 45° back extension — 3×10

### Upper B (Friday)
- Weighted chin-up — work up to 1×3 @ RPE 8 *(opener indicator)*
- DB OHP — 3×6
- Single-arm row — 3×8/side
